content.title: Rhetorical Synthesis: Completing Specific Writing Tasks
content.overview: In the Rhetorical Synthesis questions of the SAT Reading and Writing section, students are required to complete specific writing tasks based on provided notes. These tasks typically require students to filter and integrate information to achieve rhetorical goals such as introducing, summarizing, comparing, emphasizing, or providing examples.
learning_objectives: Identify the specific rhetorical goal explicitly requested in the prompt (e.g., introduce, summarize, compare).
Filter information from the notes that is directly relevant to the specific rhetorical goal.
Eliminate distractor options that are factually correct but fail to achieve the specified goal.
Construct logical and concise sentences to complete the writing task.

sections.title: Identifying Rhetorical Goals
sections.content: The instruction portion of each question clearly states the writing goal. Common instructions include: 'The student wants to introduce [topic]...', 'The student wants to summarize [topic]...', 'The student wants to emphasize a difference/similarity...' (comparison), and 'The student wants to provide an example of [topic]...'. Accurately identifying these keywords is the first step to solving the problem.

sections.title: Introduce & Summarize
sections.content: Introduction tasks usually require providing background information, such as a person's identity, the title of a work, or the basic definition of a study. Summarization tasks require covering the core points of the notes, often necessitating the extraction of commonalities across multiple note entries. A good summary option should be inclusive rather than focusing on a single detail.

sections.title: Compare & Emphasize
sections.content: Comparison tasks require mentioning two or more objects simultaneously and pointing out their similarities or differences. If the prompt asks to emphasize a specific feature (e.g., 'emphasize the uniqueness of a study'), the correct option must highlight how that feature differs from others. If an option only describes one object, even if accurately, it fails the 'compare' task.

sections.title: Provide an Example
sections.content: Example tasks require using specific facts to support a general idea or category. Students need to find specific names, data, or events in the notes and ensure these details directly prove the specific point requested by the prompt.

worked_examples.question: Notes: 1. In 1923, artist Aaron Douglas moved to New York. 2. He became a leading figure in the Harlem Renaissance. 3. His work 'The Judgment Day' blends modernism with African art elements. Task: The student wants to introduce Aaron Douglas and his major work.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Identify the goal—introduce the person and his work. Step 2: Filter information—need to include 'Aaron Douglas' and 'The Judgment Day'. Step 3: Evaluate options. Correct option example: 'Aaron Douglas was a key artist of the Harlem Renaissance whose representative work, The Judgment Day, blends multiple artistic styles.' This option achieves both the goal of introducing the person and the work.

worked_examples.question: Notes: 1. The Andromeda Galaxy is about 2.5 million light-years from Earth. 2. The Triangulum Galaxy is about 3 million light-years from Earth. Task: The student wants to emphasize the similarity in the distances of these two galaxies from Earth.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Identify the goal—emphasize similarity. Step 2: Filter information—the distance values of the two galaxies are close. Step 3: Evaluate options. Correct option example: 'The Andromeda and Triangulum galaxies are both very far from Earth, at approximately 2.5 and 3 million light-years away, respectively.' If an option says 'Andromeda is closer than Triangulum,' it emphasizes a difference, which does not meet the 'similarity' goal.

common_mistakes: Information Overload: Choosing an option that includes all information from the notes but fails to focus on the specific goal requested.
Goal Shift: The prompt asks to 'compare,' but the option only 'introduces' one object.

Factually Correct but Task Failure: The option content is entirely consistent with the notes but does not perform the rhetorical function required by the instructions (e.g., asking for an example while the option provides a summary).
exam_tips: Jump directly to the instruction: Look at the last sentence 'The student wants to...' first to clarify the goal before reading the notes.
Process of Elimination: If the prompt asks to 'emphasize a difference,' eliminate any option that does not show a comparative relationship.
Focus on transition words: Words like 'Unlike,' 'Both,' and 'Similarly' are often key markers for completing comparison or emphasis tasks.
content.recap: The key to completing Rhetorical Synthesis tasks is not understanding the deep meaning of the notes, but precisely matching the instructional requirements. By identifying keywords like 'introduce, summarize, compare, emphasize, provide an example,' extracting necessary elements from the notes, and eliminating irrelevant distractors, you can quickly lock in the correct answer.

knowledge_claims.content: When handling Rhetorical Synthesis questions, one should first read the instruction at the end of the prompt (The student wants to...) to determine the rhetorical goal.
An 'Introduce' task typically requires providing background information about the subject, such as a name, identity, or basic definition.
A 'Summarize' task requires the option to cover the core points of the notes, usually possessing high information inclusivity.
The correct option for a 'Compare' task must mention two or more objects simultaneously and explain their similarities or differences.
If the prompt asks to 'Emphasize a difference,' contrastive words such as 'unlike,' 'whereas,' or 'but' typically appear in the option.
If the prompt asks to 'Emphasize a similarity,' words such as 'both,' 'also,' or 'similarly' typically appear in the option.
A 'Provide an example' task requires using specific details from the notes (such as specific names or data) to support a broader point.
An option is incorrect if it fails to achieve the specified rhetorical goal, even if its facts perfectly match the content of the notes.
When completing a task to 'emphasize a specific feature,' check if the option places that feature at the core of the sentence or uses an emphatic tone.
'Summarizing' focuses on extracting commonalities or overall descriptions, while 'providing an example' focuses on showing specific individuals or cases.
Rhetorical Synthesis questions do not require students to use outside knowledge; all information needed for the correct answer must come from the provided notes.
When instructions ask to 'introduce and summarize,' the correct option must include both background identity information and the main content of the research or work.
